limits: Matching is on drug counts per level, not on training rows.
Retrospective; no mechanism, clinical or drug-choice claim.

the_answer_refines_C113.finding: both annotations beat their own size-matched nulls, so neither gain is a bin-size artefact
the_answer_refines_C113.reading: both real partitions add value that a size-matched random partition does not (+0.005 and +0.009, both spanning zero). So pathway versus target is a MAGNITUDE difference, roughly two to one, not a difference between content and no content.

this_changes_the_practical_rule.after: prefer pathway because it is worth about twice as much, and treat target as a genuine, weaker fallback when a drug has no pathway label. Target is not worthless; it is just half as informative.
this_changes_the_practical_rule.what_would_have_made_it_the_simpler_rule: if target had failed to beat its own null, the rule would have been 'only pathway carries content'
this_changes_the_practical_rule.why_that_mattered: the two rules give different advice for a drug that has a target annotation but no pathway annotation

the_nulls_are_both_near_zero.reading: matching the size distribution of a random partition leaves it indistinguishable from identity, for both annotation types. That is the control doing its job twice.

a_bug_i_caught_before_filing.symptom: every contrast involving the identity arm came out as NaN in the first run
a_bug_i_caught_before_filing.cause: the identity arm's prediction is constant on this pool, so spearmanr returns NaN, and I had not guarded that for the three main arms
a_bug_i_caught_before_filing.fix: record 0 when the correlation is undefined, as I do elsewhere
a_bug_i_caught_before_filing.note: the three contrasts that did not touch identity were already correct, which is why the substantive answer was visible before the fix
